newsitem.title: UK: French poll puts EMU bonds trades in a spin.
newsitem.headline: French poll puts EMU bonds trades in a spin.

text.p: European bond market convergence trades have been turned upside down by the surprise left-wing victory in the first round of French parliamentary elections, strategists said on Tuesday.
Instead of yields of peripheral European bonds falling to German levels, Bunds now face the prospect of rising yields to meet peripherals, they said.
"The whole nature of convergence will be very different this time round to last year," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW.
"It's going to be all about German yields moving up towards peripheral Europe as European Monetary Union (EMU) risk is priced into the core."

French President Jacques Chirac's election gamble went disastrously wrong last Sunday when the opposition left chalked up 44 percent of the votes, when counting the Greens, leaving the ruling centre-right coalition and other moderate rightists with only 36.5 percent.
But the race is still wide open ahead of the second and final round next Sunday, with the difference in seats between the two blocs equivalent to less than one percentage point of the popular vote.

But whoever now forms the next government, the chances of EMU going ahead on schedule with strict adherence to the Maastricht criteria have been dealt a blow with talk of a soft euro buzzing through markets as a result.
And convergence trades will have to adjust accordingly, analysts said.
Steve Major, head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais, said convergence trades would now likely take place at a higher nominal level -- maybe 50 basis points higher on 10-year yields.

Reed said investors should look to the front end of Spain for lucrative convergence trades under the new regime. "We'll now have to start thinking of the Spanish market as being inside of EMU," she said.

"The spread around the two year level is still around 100 basis points over Germany, and will have to come down one way or another in the next 18 months. So that's really the best value for convergence."
Major said the root of market fears was that a socialist victory would imply a more lenient approach by France to the convergence criteria necessary for EMU.
There are also concerns of possible political control of the European Central Bank (ECB) and the perception the French left would favour a wider EMU from the outset, possibly including Italy.
Some strategists suggested investors make a swift exit from European bond markets altogether, but if they do remain, to avoid the usual rush into German Bunds.
Major said ironically, French OATs were a better bet going into Sunday's run-off, rather than Bunds -- usually the first port of call in times of EMU strife.
"I wouldn't necessarily go into Bunds. A more spongy euro is negative for the mark and there's a very high concentration of foreign ownership in Bunds," he said.
"If I had to hold anything, I'd sooner hold OATs."
Major said strong domestic ownership of French bonds, coupled with a stack of cash waiting to flood in at cheaper levels, underpinned the market.
He suggested shortening duration in a defensive bid to guard against EMU turmoil.
"If the left-wing win on Sunday, it has to be seen as negative so I'd take a reduced duration stance in Europe," he said.

Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London, agreed a defensive strategy was the way to play the final French vote, but suggested Germany and Britain were the places to be on a spread basis.

He also noted domestic investment propping up the French market, and said support for the 10-year OAT/Bund spread would kick in around minus five basis points. By 1040 GMT, 10-year OATs were yielding nine basis points less than equivalent Bunds.
